newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Foxtel says Australia pay tv changes to take time.
newsitem.headline: Foxtel says Australia pay tv changes to take time.

text.p: Loss-making pay television operator Foxtel said on Thursday its two shareholders News Corp Ltd and state-owned Telstra Corp were not losing patience with the business and that major changes to the industry might take some time.

"I think they have both been very committed and very satisfied with results like today," Foxtel chief executive Tom Mockeridge told Reuters. Foxtel said earlier it had 200,000 subscribers, a rise of 50,000 in the past four months.
Foxtel and Australia's two other main pay-TV operators, Optus Vision and Australis Media Ltd, are suffering heavy losses, fuelling expectations of an industry shake-up.
Optus Vision is said to be negotiating a merger with Australis, seen by analysts as the most vulnerable to takeover, and it is speculated Foxtel is also in talks with Australis.
Mockridge declined to comment on the rumour but said Foxtel already had a programming deal with Australis and there were other areas where Foxtel and Australis could cooperate.
"We have been talking to all sorts of people in theindustry and I won't bite on anything specific," he said.
"I think...that compared with last year when there was lots of probably unnecessary acrimony between the players, this year a bit of maybe common sense has gone into the place."
But Mockridge said an industry shake-up was not inevitable and that growth in total pay TV subscriptions was phenomonal.
"Across the distributers there are more than 600,000 people buying a service today, which is a penetration rate of about 10 percent in less than two years," he added.
He forecast total subcriber numbers could approach one million in Australia in 12 months and said a number of pay TV operators could ultimately become viable.

An agreed shake-up of the industry would be such a complex task, given the rival programming contracts and cable investments which would need to be sorted out, that observers should expect a sudden announcement, he said.
"They are expecting major changes," Mockridge said.
"But it's a very complex picture and I just don't think you are going to wake up one morning and find that happen," he added.
The two big telecommunications companies exposed to the industry, Telstra and rival Optus Communications Pty Ltd, are negotiating to rationalise the cable networks delivering pay TV.
Optus Communications wholly owns Optus Vision, and calls for the parent to sell its pay-TV unit are growing as Optus Communications prepares to float on the Australian share market.
A one-third stake of Telstra is also due to be offered to the public in November, and the success of its float is seen to hinge partly on securing a cable-sharing deal with Optus.
Telstra and Optus are investing a total A$7 billion in rolling out duplicate optic-fibre cable networks for no return so far.
Their strategy so far has been to use pay-TV as a way of tempting households to connect to the networks, which would later pump interactive and telephony services into the home.
Foxtel reported an operating loss of A$98 million for the six months ended December 31, and Mockeridge said there would be "no surprises" in the second half-year ending June 30.
Foxtel will not turn a profit "for a while", Mockeridge said. But he denied News and Telstra were losing patience.
"In the end, it depends what you call viable and the only people who can determine whether anything is viable are the shareholders...News and Telstra are very committed to Foxtel."

Optus Communications is owned 24.9 percent by Australia's Mayne Nickeless Ltd and 24.5 percent each by Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc and U.S. telecom BellSouth Corp. The rest is owned by Australian institutions.
-- Mark Bendeich, Melbourne bureau 613-9286-1421
